title: Multi-Scale Diffusion-Guided Graph Learning for Multi-View Clustering
one_liner: When you have the same objects shown in different ways, blend them smartly by diffusing connectivity across views and filtering out misleading pairs.
lead: Imagine you have photos of a car from different angles, plus thermal and radar versions — each view gives a partial picture. The task is to group cars that look similar across all views. Current methods struggle because (1) they lock in a fixed graph of connections, (2) they mistakenly say two distant cars are similar just to have a contrasting pair, and (3) balancing global patterns with local detail is hard.

paras: Multi-view clustering needs to find groups across many versions of the data. Today's graph-based methods treat the connection map like a fixed blueprint — once built, it stays rigid. A fixed graph misses what really matters: as you blend information from views, the best connections shift and strengthen, but a frozen map cannot adapt.

A beginner tries this: for each view, build a graph connecting similar items, then mix the graphs. But in contrastive learning (a technique that learns by comparing pairs), you need negative examples — items that are definitely different. The problem: you accidentally pick two distant cars that are actually the same in reality and call them negative, which poisons the learning signal. Finally, keeping all views aligned while letting each view shine differently pulls in opposite directions — a classical trade-off.

callout.html: Adapt the connection map through diffusion steps, filter out fake negatives using likely paths, and balance views by sharing structural cores.

steps.text: Blur and sharpen the similarity graph across multiple time steps, fusing fine and coarse patterns.

steps.b: Disorder-guided fusion (entropy: how spread-out is the pattern)
steps.text: Measure disorder in each step; weight them to capture both local clusters and global shape.
Trace probable paths through the evolved graph; use them to downweight unlikely negative pairs.
Apply a smooth decay curve to contrastive targets, so common mistakes matter less than clear errors.

steps.b: Shared structural core (embeddings: shared numerical descriptions)
steps.text: Align all views on a common structure; each view adds its own flavor without breaking the core.

paras: The method rewrites two things: the graph of connections itself (making it evolve over multiple diffusion steps instead of staying frozen) and how negative pairs are chosen for contrastive learning (filtering out false negatives using random walk probability).

hidden.name: Diffused similarity across time steps
paras: As diffusion progresses, the graph transforms: edges that connect true peers grow brighter, edges to noise fade. This evolving map is the hidden quantity — it sits between the raw similarity (too noisy) and a fixed graph (too rigid). The paper measures it by computing how disorder (entropy) in each step's pattern changes, then combining the steps that carry the most structure.

A random walk explores high-probability paths — routes that a random traveler would naturally follow. If two items are close in reality, a random walk finds them easily; if they are false neighbors, the walk avoids them. This probability guides which negative pairs to trust.

heat.caption: Darker means clearer signal. Diffusion sharpens structure over steps.

reads.html: Diffusion is like gently shaking a blurry photo — details emerge as noise settles.
The paper fuses diffusion matrices at multiple scales using entropy-weighted aggregation.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the three-part machine
paras: Part 1: Diffusion evolves the graph. In early steps, noise spreads as much as signal; in later steps, only strong connections survive. By collecting steps with high entropy (clear structure), the method captures both the fine texture (which items cluster tightly) and the big shape (which clusters are distinct). This is richer than one frozen graph.

Part 2: Random walk filters negatives. In contrastive learning, you learn by comparing each item to a positive (same group) and negatives (different groups). But the method does not know ground truth, so it might label two really-similar items as different by accident. A random walk naturally avoids unlikely bridges — walks along high-probability paths. Items that a walk reaches easily are likely true neighbors; distant items that only connect through low-probability detours are probably false negatives. Down-weighting false negatives removes the poison from training.

Part 3: Shared embeddings balance views. Each view is unique, but they must agree on the core structure — which items group together. The method learns a shared embedding that all views see, forcing alignment. Then each view learns its own flavor on top. This reconciles the push-and-pull: global consistency (shared core) plus local detail (view-specific features).

Learn shared structure plus view flavor

math.words: loss equals contrastive similarity minus scaled negative similarity, with adaptive weights from random walk probability
math.equation: L = -log(exp(sim(x,x+) / tau) / (exp(sim(x,x+) / tau) + sum_neg w(neg) * exp(sim(x,neg) / tau)))
symbols: how similar item x is to a true match
how similar item x is to a wrong pairing
weight for that negative, from random walk probability
add up all the weighted negatives

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose x is a red car in view 1, x+ is the same car in view 2 (true match), and neg1, neg2 are two blue cars in view 2.
sim(x, x+) = 0.9 (high, they match). sim(x, neg1) = 0.6, sim(x, neg2) = 0.4.

Random walk finds a clear route to neg1 (common blue model) but only a weak bridge to neg2 (rare blue variant). So w(neg1) = 0.8, w(neg2) = 0.2 (down-weighted because it is probably a false negative).
Loss = -log(2718 / (2718 + 333)) = -log(0.89) ≈ 0.12. The true match dominates, and the fake negative is safely suppressed.

math.note: The random walk weights downgrade false negatives, so the loss focuses on learning real structure, not noise.

charts.title: Old method (fixed graph + all negatives)
charts.note: Each view works alone, but they do not align. False negatives hurt learning.

charts.title: MANGO (diffusion + filtered negatives + shared core)
charts.note: All views improve because diffusion makes the connection map sharper; consistency soars because the shared embeddings force agreement. Diffusion and filtering do the heavy lifting.

items.html: If one view is a thermal image and another is radio-wave data, the shared structure may be too loose to anchor them. Entropy guidance helps focus on clear steps, but if signal-to-noise is low in a view (many false connections mixed with real ones), that view's poor-quality graph contaminates the fused result, because every view influences the shared embeddings equally.
Too few steps miss global structure; too many wash out local detail. The entropy weights must be chosen carefully, or the fused graph is a useless blur.
If the input graph is wildly wrong (e.g., all items look equally similar), the random walk cannot distinguish likely from unlikely paths, so false-negative filtering does nothing.
When views have complementary detail, entropy is well-calibrated, and the input graphs have real signal, diffusion and filtering sharpen multi-view agreement dramatically.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic dataset: 5 item clusters, 3 views (each view scrambles the order slightly and adds noise). Train a simple graph network with MANGO. Compare: (1) the final clustering purity (fraction of correct assignments), (2) the agreement between views (how often all three views assign the same item to the same cluster), and (3) the count of false negatives that were downweighted by random walk filtering.
demo.metric_eq: purity = (correct cluster assignments) / (total items); cross_view_agreement = (assignments all views agree on) / (total items); false_neg_filtered = (negatives downweighted below 0.3) / (total negatives considered)
demo.closing: The demo must show: purity climbs (diffusion finds structure), cross-view agreement rises (shared embeddings align views), and many false negatives are safely pruned (random walk filtering works).
